We present an enhanced semantics for the graph programming language GP2, evolving from its predecessor's approach. This transition facilitates the emergence of unstable oscillatory perturbations that reorganize the current profile to create magnetic null points, thereby generating the characteristic palm tree pattern. Consequently, these numerical outcomes align with experimental observations from JET regarding the stability and structure of PTMs observed at multiple null points.

The rise of distributed networks has intensified the need for privacy protection. In Federated Learning (FL), where users train models on sensitive data without sharing raw information, ensuring privacy remains a critical challenge. Similarly, in blockchain systems, protecting user identities and their data is equally essential. Federated Learning combined with Local Differential Privacy (FLDPL) represents a promising distributed framework for handling private data across users. This architecture allows aggregation of noisy data generated at each user's device, thereby mitigating individual privacy risks. On the other hand, implementing LDP within traditional blockchans (LPBC) serves as a leading distributed secure solution. In this approach, users transmit obfuscated data to a central aggregator, which then generates and broadcasts a protected data set to all participants. This study presents a unified architecture that integrates FL and LBDP networks, leveraging the privacy and security strengths of FL with FLDPL alongside the blockchain capabilities found in LPBC. By merging these three key components, the proposed framework enhances overall privacy protection across distributed environments.

In 1947, George Dantzig introduced the well-known simplex algorithm for solving linear programming (LP), along with a vertex (facet) pivoting technique that remains in use today. Although effective, this standard method suffers from exponential complexity in the worst-case scenario and can exhibit poor performance in practice. This work introduces an alternative, facet-based pivoting approach. Instead of moving along the edges of a polygonal chain linking successive extreme points, it traverses the faces of a cell chain to explore the solution space. Our proposed cell pivot algorithm leverages the internal structure and topology to resolve problems more rapidly. Experimental results on randomly generated problem instances demonstrate that this cell pivot method surpasses both the classical simplex algorithm and its modern variants in efficiency.

This study explores the impact of the Higgs boson's inherent width on the differential distributions used when the Higgs decays into a top-antitop ($t\bar{t}$) pair. We also calculate various systematic uncertainties, such as those arising from scale variations and experimental detector effects, on both full and narrow approximation calculations. We also show that these uncertainties are not the primary cause of the observed variations in differential distributions.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) facilitate effective node classification by leveraging both node attributes and network topology. Yet, their reliance on vast amounts of labeled data means poor labels can lead to erroneous predictions. Consequently, explanation methods have gained traction to offer post-hoc insights into GNN predictions, thereby enhancing model transparency and understanding. While prior approaches like PGExplainer attempt to emulate neighbor selection throughout the training process using gradient analysis to explain node-level predictions, they often neglect the influence of specific nodes and the sensitivity of the model to those choices. In this work, we reimagine PGExplainer through a lens of "global" node feature probing, moving beyond the local neighbor selection paradigm. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have demonstrated success in solving inverse problems within sparse data settings. Collectively, these findings suggest that perceptions of this continuum are primarily driven by independent contributions from visual categorizability and agency.

The evaluation of vector magnetic field structures in vector-spectrum images is essential for understanding solar physics. This process typically involves two steps: initially, identifying the orientation of the solar photosphere's magnetic field to create a full disk map, and then, deriving the actual magnetic field strength from the estimated inclination. This paper focuses on the latter, aiming to enhance the precision of field strength measurements from spectromagnetic images by explicitly incorporating magnetic fill fraction. By applying this method to a full disk map of the fill fraction alongside a previously published full disk map of the transverse component ($B_t$), we developed a new, improved map of the radial component ($B_r$). When the $B_r$ map derived from the JPL/UVIT mission is divided by the JPL/UVIT full disk map of the radial component ($B_{JPL}$), the resulting map closely resembles the NSO/NVT map derived from a simulation that includes a realistic magnetic filling factor. This approach offers a significant improvement over the simplistic division of $B_r$ by the observed $B_r$, which fails to account for magnetic fill fraction and thus produces a map that does not align well with the National Solar Observatory (NSO)/NVT data. This improved method offers a more accurate estimation of the true magnetic field strength.

This study examines a peer-to-peer energy trading framework within demand side management, where a group of consumers exchanges electricity through a central aggregator. Consumers act as rational consumers seeking to minimize their individual costs, modeled as a non-cooperative game. We prove that when consumers have identical preferences, a Nash equilibrium always exists. Our results distinguish between two scenarios based on the presence or absence of a central unit. In cases where a central unit exists, consumers strive to minimize personal energy bills; conversely, in decentralized setups, consumers aim to minimize generation and consumption costs. Our primary goal is to develop strategies for distributed implementation, enabling consumers to reach a Nash equilibrium using only local information exchange. We demonstrate that, in environments with a central unit, consumers can achieve the Nash equilibrium by sharing only their current time-step energy consumption data. In contrast, in decentralized environments, we present an adaptive distributed algorithm utilizing frequency as a coordination signal, allowing consumers to converge to the Nash equilibrium through updates based solely on neighbor interactions.

A key aspect of studying quantum gravity (QG) is determining how these effects alter the thermodynamic properties of black holes. Our analysis shows that in regimes where quantum gravity is significant, the stability behavior of charged black strings changes, particularly within Rastall theory. We ultimately conclude that the core objective of quantum gravity research is to understand how these effects fundamentally modify the stability characteristics of black holes.

We have conducted a comprehensive study examining the correlations between Fe II flux ratios and Fe/H relative iron abundances in the A0V star HD 147513, which is known to host a transiting exoplanet. Additionally, we applied this correlation to derive the total iron abundance, yielding log Fe/H = -3.90 ± 0.05. We subsequently applied the same methodology to examine Fe II lines in the optical spectrum of HD 147513, utilizing the same standard for consistency. This approach enabled us to calculate the iron abundance independently, resulting in log Fe/H = -3.91 ± 0.04. The strong agreement between these two values demonstrates that the identified correlation between stellar abundance and flux ratios is a robust and reliable tool for the classification of stars.

Morphological complexity is a fundamental yet difficult concept in linguistics, with debates regarding its definition, measurement, and validation persisting since the pioneering work of Greenberg and Holman. We explore the correlation between these complexity measures and a array of typological variables, as well as the frequency with which such complexity is used in corpora. Kernel methods have been extensively employed to address challenges in data analysis. Among them, methods that project datasets into high-dimensional spaces using the kernel trick have proven particularly effective. In this study, we introduce an modification to the Arithmetico-Geometric Mean (AGM) algorithm by incorporating a nonlinear function termed *m-ar-K*. This function serves as a unified approach capable of recovering several known kernels as specific instances when appropriate parameters are selected. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the use of *m-ar-K* in set-arithmetic operations allows for the application of these techniques to perform efficient dimensionality reduction. We show that this approach yields data projections into significantly higher dimensions than standard strategies, thereby preventing information degradation. Numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of *m-ar-K* kernels across various tasks, validating their promise for future research and development.

Detecting moving objects and identifying events from video is a crucial challenge in computer vision and vision-based interaction systems. This work introduces a proposed system designed to detect spatio-temporal events from camera-captured sequences. The approach links events to "world space" characteristics, enabling the model to account for their varying spatial resolutions regardless of whether events originate from a single image frame or multiple frames. The system utilizes a neural network to identify specific events, which relies on a set of spatial features. These features are derived by analyzing the features of all pixels within an initial network pass, leveraging foreground segmentation and motion analysis to create necessary input data. This feature derivation proves effective for multi-camera setups and handles events of varying magnitudes. The system is configured to support the model learning of these features through either supervised training or self-supervised learning mechanisms. When trained using supervision, the method is demonstrated capable of inferring events driven by domain-specific knowledge. The detection mechanism itself combines the feature set with temporal matching logic to determine occurrences. Evaluated against various scenarios, this approach achieves an accuracy of 99% in identifying single events and 95% when detecting concurrent events across all frames. Furthermore, when supporting self-supervised learning, this technique successfully infers events purely based on raw imagery without prior labels. This outcome is validated by a qualitative review showing correct event inference across different scenarios and a single metric of 70% accuracy for self-learning applications.

Understanding dialogues requires language models to recognize semantic connections between consecutive turns. This study reimagines dialogue modeling as a multi-turn semantic relationship detection task. We introduce an ensemble of leading conversational models enhanced with explicit semantic relation labels, utilizing these models as annotators to teach the system through self-training. This approach models conversations explicitly using semantic labels without requiring a separate human annotator, effectively leveraging automated labeling capabilities. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on both local tasks, including turn-level prediction, response generation, and character-level sentiment analysis, as well as global tasks, specifically multi-turn emotion and sentiment detection. Furthermore, we conduct experiments examining how models perform across varying numbers of training turns, providing empirical evidence and insights into how multi-turn semantic relations influence the detection of these features during multi-turn interactions.

As machine learning algorithms become increasingly sophisticated, they are also growing more opaque, creating a conflict between their predictive capabilities and their transparency. This issue has highlighted the need for research into trustworthy, fair, and accountable algorithms, placing a central emphasis on algorithmic interpretability. While the importance of this field is now widely acknowledged, the specific meaning of"interpretability"remains elusive and debated. Various stakeholders, including regulators, developers, and end-users, require different levels of understanding, yet current approaches often prioritize statistical explanations for model predictions. Consequently, fundamental questions remain unanswered: Does understanding how a specific algorithm functions equate to comprehension, and can truly sophisticated, sophisticated models remain understandable? In the following, we explore the concept of algorithmic interpretability from a human-centric perspective. We highlight how the requirements for interpretability shift depending on the task, the user involved, and the algorithm employed, and we introduce a new challenge: "algorithmic incoherence," where an algorithm's internal logic diverges from human intuition, thereby complicating genuine comprehension.

The Isolation Forest (iF) algorithm operates on the premise that anomalies reside far from the majority of data points in feature space. Its scoring mechanism, defined as $s(x) = 2^{-\hat v_n(x)}$, derives from the average path length to isolate point $x$, where $\hat v_n(x)$ relies on normalized average distances within isolation trees. Despite these assumptions, the theoretical justification linking the individual score $s(x)$ to the anomaly probability remains unclear. This paper introduces an alternative anomaly scoring function, $s'(x) = \|x - c_T\|^2 / \hat d_n(x)^2$, designed to reflect how unlikely it is for a point $x$ to reside within the data manifold. We provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that, specifically for linearly separable high-dimensional data generated by subspaces, our revised metric $s'(x)$ possesses validity. Empirical evaluations on synthetic datasets confirm that our proposed function outperforms the traditional $s(x)$, while tests on real-world benchmarks illustrate comparable competitive capabilities.

Extremal value statistics is a key component in the analysis of data characterized by the most significant observations. To address these deficiencies, this paper introduces a straightforward yet robust method for both predicting new values (conditional) and identifying extreme thresholds for detection purposes (marginal). Rooted in a straightforward Exponential Generalized Linear Model, the proposed approach utilizes a conjugate Normal-Gamma prior combined with a Gamma process to yield closed-form posterior solutions. These analytical solutions facilitate rapid convergence, enabling the application of Bayesian methods to datasets with minimum dimensions of 1,000 records. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are among the most extensively utilized generative models. In VAEs, the posterior distribution of the latent variables often encompasses numerous irrelevant dimensions that do not capture the essential features required for decoding. We introduce Sparse VAEs to address this issue by integrating the principles of Sparse Principal Component Analysis into the standard VAE framework. We further demonstrate empirically that these methods significantly increase the effective dimensionality and sparsity of the learned latent representations while enhancing the quality of generated samples and the decoding performance. Topological phase transitions in high-order topological insulators (OTIs) are characterized by the emergence or annihilation of bulk mobility gaps and bulk topological sidebands. This study demonstrates that in quasicrystalline gratings—a prototypical model for OTIs—disorder within this environment narrows the bulk mobility gaps, resulting in enriched phase diagrams. Notably, the bulk mobility gap reactions occur at distinct quasicrystal parameters compared to the gap closures of edge states, creating a specific edge-bulk mobility gap framework. Our analysis indicates that while the bulk mobility gap collapses due to the closure of the bulk sidebands, bulk topological sidebands can also vanish independently. Consequently, these observations confirm the existence of unique topological phases specific to quasicrystalline structures. Ultimately, bulk and edge phase diagrams serve as a reliable indicator for identifying topological phase transitions in OTIs, distinguishing between bulk and edge topological phases.

Inference of gene regulatory networks relies heavily on determining the most relevant predictive variables for each target variable. This study introduces "Relevance Learning with Applications to Gene Networks" (RLALAG), a novel approach designed to identify key predictive variables within time-dependent expression data sets. The method's core innovation is modeling variable relevance across different time points for the entire dataset and utilizing these relevance scores to guide sampling strategies. This adaptive sampling process prioritizes generating samples in regions associated with higher relevance, which significantly enhances computational efficiency. Empirical analysis indicates that RLALAG achieves superior performance compared to established methods like LASSO, RFE, and Random Forests in detecting highly concentrated, sparse relevant groups in time-dependent gene expression data. Furthermore, using RLALAG to deduce the structure of the human C. elegans embryonic gene network demonstrated high accuracy and alignment with recent findings. Finally, both the underlying algorithms and corresponding user-friendly software are accessible via the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengzheng1983/RLALAG.

Telepresence robots are increasingly popular across diverse sectors, including education and healthcare. Transfer learning is a standard approach in machine vision that leverages pre-trained deep neural networks (DNNs) to new, unseen tasks. Although base features acquired from training on large datasets like ImageNet are typically transferred to these DNNs, a critical question remains: which specific layers constitute these transferred features? Our study addresses this by examining how features from different layers of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) transfer across diverse tasks. We demonstrate that transferability is not confined to early layers, which primarily handle fundamental imagery, nor is it guaranteed in later layers. Instead, mid-level layers appear to be the most transferable. To identify transferred features, we propose a new metric that assesses feature similarity between source and target networks. Our analysis of multiple architectures and several application domains reveals that features with broader applicability encompass a wider variety of visual concepts. Furthermore, our findings show an inverse relationship between feature discriminability and generalizability: as the number of concepts a feature set represents increases, its ability to distinguish individual images diminishes.

In multmodal systems, integrating knowledge modalities enhances robustness and accuracy in the face of noise and missing data. However, this combination is not always feasible. We introduce a systematic approach to determine an optimal subset of modalities that balances performance with cost, formally treating it as a Fixed-Cost Subset Selection problem under the assumption of additive noise. In a cost-limited context, we must weigh the advantages of high-performing sensors that are susceptible to noise against lower-performing, unaffected ones. The profound success of Transformers in diverse downstream applications has been driven by their superior capability to capture long-term dependencies, a feat achieved through the parallel processing inherent in the self-attention mechanism. To address this bottleneck, we introduce the Backward Dropping Algorithm, which stochastically eliminates a subset of tokens from the input sequence during each training iteration. This technique effectively simulates scenarios where only specific portions of the data are observable at various stages, compelling the model to infer missing parts by leveraging information from other retained tokens and encouraging the learning of dependencies across the full dataset. Empirical results on language modeling tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms standard training strategies, with improvements becoming more pronounced as sequence lengths increase. Furthermore, we validate the robustness of this approach across other applications, including machine translation and image caption generation.

Nevertheless, most generative models depend heavily on large-scale annotated datasets, which are often expensive and time-consuming to acquire. This paper presents a new generative framework that enables the learning of effective models using only unlabelled data. Our approach employs two key strategies: first, it utilizes a discriminator to restrict the model's output to a feasible region of the latent space; second, it enhances training efficiency through a multi-stage process involving pre-training, fine-tuning, and optimization. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method yields performance comparable to existing approaches while eliminating the requirement for annotated resources.

This research examines how the effective spectral density, $J(\omega)$, of the photonic bath influences the nonequilibrium dissipative phase transition within a single-mode Bose–Hubbert model. We demonstrate that the interference patterns emerging from the second-order autocorrelation and holographic measurement of the photonic bath influence both the homogeneous and heterogeneous parts of the phase transition—specifically, that the Fourier components corresponding to photon-number HBT correlations and those reflecting phase HBT correlations directly affect their respective branches. We construct a theoretical framework to calculate the exponents of this nonequilibrium phase transition and evaluate how different forms of dissipation modify the critical exponent values for this driven, open system in comparison to its isolated counterpart.

We present a novel probabilistic approach to segmenting brain tissues in medical images, leveraging Gaussian Processes (GPs) to model both the segmentation boundaries and their uncertainties. Unlike medially defined models constrained to 3D centered manifolds with topological restrictions, our GP-based segmentation allows for asymmetric, or even absent, model structures while avoiding such topological limitations. Furthermore, by treating the GP as a probabilistic framework, our approach naturally quantifies uncertainty regarding the segmentation results. We validate our approach on two distinct data sets: first, synthetic medially defined models derived from previously described methods, and second, real-world 3D confocal micromorphology data of islets of Langerhans acquired via laser ablation scanning.

A one-dimensional Bose gas is subjected to dissipation via its interaction with a thermal environment while simultaneously undergoing Floquet driving, a scenario where bath-induced dissipation competes with Floquet heating. By utilizing a phenomenological approach, this work investigates the time evolution of two-body correlations in the quasi-free regime to examine the conditions necessary for driven Bose condensation. Under the asymptotic steady state, a stable state emerges where the balance between driving and dissipation results in Bose condensation even within high-temperature thermal baths.

This research examines the impact of inelastic photon scattering on two-level quantum systems within atomic fountains and resonators, focusing on how this phenomenon affects the precision of ultrafast lasers and optical fountains. It demonstrates that photonic detection can substantially boost the precision of ultrafast laser-based fountains compared to traditional microwave systems. Detection facilitates better state discrimination, surpassing the limits of scattering-free free induction periods and enabling sampling frequencies far above the free induction decay rate. Additionally, inelastic photon scattering in a Ramsey interferometer fountains can reach negligible levels under specific detection conditions, surpassing standard Ramsey sensitivity, provided that detection occurs within a specific time window. This finding establishes a significantly "smoother" sampling window for detectors-based quantum fountains compared to the durations required by Ramsey, scattering-free free induction decay methods. This paper further quantifies the impact of dark state-based photonic detection strategies on sampling frequency enhancements and state stability in optical fountains, demonstrating how targeted detection approaches minimize inelastic scattering events to improve overall system performance.

This study presents a novel framework, Loss Gradient Decomposition (LGD), designed to enhance image retrieval. The core concept of LGD involves splitting standard pair-wise loss into a base component and an adaptive component. By applying gradient descent separately based on this decomposition, the method enables effective training even without data augmentation. We analyze the structural morphology of tensor networks (TNs) by identifying the elementary operations they facilitate to information. By rephrasing TNs as functional tools for processing data via tensor operations, we derive a universal protocol for constructing these networks around specific tensor types. This method yields rigorous constraints on the geometry and topology of TNs. Our analysis demonstrates that any code defined as a single tensor type must be either a repetition or a parity code when viewed as an erasure correction scheme. Furthermore, we examine how a specific unitary transformation applied to an underlying tensor generates a new code capable of correcting distinct error syndromes, leading to the identification of a class of codes where the logical operations are natively expressed as tensor contractions.

Radio filaments in the Galaxy are magnetized structures with a linear aspect ratio of roughly 100, yet their origins remain unexplained. We suggest that magnetic filamentation arises from either (a) a universal magnetohydrodynamic instability in a uniform field or (b) the radial expansion of an initially uniform magnetic field. In the first model, the instability of a rotating cylinder yields a characteristic length scale, $L \approx 10^5 B_0^{-1/2}$ pc (where $B_0$ is the initial field strength in $\mu$G). Matching the observed average spacing of filaments ($\sim$100 pc) within this framework implies a universal mean magnetic field strength of 30 mG across the radio filaments. While this implies such strong magnetization is unlikely for the source region, it can occur if the initial field possessed significant flux tangential to the expansion direction. Under the second mechanism, radial expansion from a central point naturally produces filamentation in regions of low or zero tangential pressure. Consequently, the pattern of filaments in the radio sky likely results from multiple outflows originating from various sources.

The leader-follower approach is a straightforward, communication-efficient method for managing distributed energy resources (DERs) within smart grids, particularly when coordination is difficult among DERs. In this framework, a leader entity optimizes its dispatch based on aggregated measurements from followers (loads), while treating each individual load as a distinct entity; however, due to the "lost-in-the-middleman" effect, traditional strategies often fail to accurately reflect the true real-time power demand of every follower, leading to suboptimal grid outcomes. To address this, we introduce a demand aggregation mechanism that enhances the grid's response accuracy. By integrating a nonlinear gain within the leader-follower architecture, our solution significantly reduces demand estimation errors and mitigates overshoots or undershoots frequently observed in conventional methods. We validate these findings through simulations on both the IEEE 34-bus distribution network and ISO-NE load profiles.

This study investigates a stochastic setting for the Optimistic Upper Confidence Bound (UCB2) algorithm within the context of the Multi-Armed Bandit problem. Unlike standard stochastic assumptions, our model accounts for arms becoming temporarily unavailable. We analyze this model by establishing a theoretical lower bound on regret that incorporates both the worst-case losses and delays associated with arm selection. To our knowledge, this represents the initial work to explicitly quantify such regret in terms of both loss and delay for the most detrimental arm. Additionally, we demonstrate that the optimistic UCB2 approach, which is originally known to be effective in stochastic environments, proves robust against these theoretical challenges.

We introduce a novel theoretical framework for text-generation within dialogue that is both computationally efficient and highly adaptable. This model stands out due to its compact yet powerful, computationally efficient structure and its capacity to accommodate an extensive range of adaptable fields, including but not limited to stance detection in dialogue and multi-turn dialogue systems. Further experiments demonstrate that our model outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in these specific adaptive scenarios. We anticipate this model will serve as robust baseline, paving the way for future advancements in various text-generating applications driven by dialogue.

For decades, the study of hadrons and their interactions dominated quantum chromodynamics (QCD), until the field discovered a new frontier in strong-interaction matter at both extremely high densities and low temperatures, as well as very low densities under extreme conditions. This discovery prompted a quest for the equation of state of this strong-interaction matter, driving progress in the QCD phase diagram. Recently, the study of quark–antiquark bound states (quarkonium) has emerged as an increasingly significant tool for understanding these phases. This review examines recent advancements in using quarkonium as a probe to explore the QCD phase diagram, highlighting progress in theoretical models and phenomenological analyses, particularly regarding the suppression of quarkonium in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. The article further explores the potential of using quarkonium to investigate the first-order hadronic phase transition and the nature of the critical endpoint within the high-density, low-temperature region accessible via colliders. Finally, the properties of bound states near the critical point are discussed.

This study establishes a fully nonlinear fully stochastic simulation framework to examine the impact of inflow turbulence and irregular waves on the variability of fatigue loads and extreme forces on offshore wind turbines. The research highlights the significance of the spatial and temporal coherence characteristics of turbulent wind fields, as well as irregular wave fields, on load fluctuations. Spatial and temporal resolution requirements for stochastic wind and wave fields are specified to ensure accurate probability density function (PDF) calculations for turbine loads. By synthesizing these results, the paper underscores that mean structural loads are primarily governed by the mean spatial distribution of the stochastic inflow field, whereas load deviations (fluctuations) depend on the second-order statistics of those inflow fields.

We introduce a strategy to automatically map the evolution of public sentiment regarding COVID-19, utilizing natural language processing and topic modeling. This method analyzes survey data from across 16 nations to examine shifting public mood. Specifically, we employ latent Dirichlet allocation to identify salient themes within the responses, while a sentiment analysis pipeline detects shifts in emotional tone. By integrating these two elements, our approach offers a nuanced, topic-sensitive perspective on how sentiment fluctuates over the course of the pandemic. It serves as a valuable asset for public health authorities, enabling a deeper comprehension of collective attitudes and the rapid detection of emerging concerns.

Optimal experimental designs are vital for maximizing information extraction from tests and minimizing the effort required to reach significant scientific conclusions. In contrast, inverse problems seek to deduce specific model parameters by fitting their predictions to existing data. This study introduces a novel method that unifies experimental design and model parameter inversion by leveraging the solutions to the optimal inverse problem. By doing so, this approach enhances the interpretation of intricate ultrafast experiments dealing with high-dimensional control fields and high-order response variables. Notably, this optimal inversion strategy effectively manages the challenges associated with high-noise, limited-sample data and addresses the "ill-posedness" inherent in inverse problems through a cost function that integrates the correlations between the data and the underlying model. Validated through a closed-system, high-dimensional quantum system, this optimal inversion method has been extended to address open systems.

This study presents an novel, novel approach for automatically analyzing driving scenarios involving multiple vehicles. Specifically, it introduces a novel joint probabilistic data association (JPDA)-based tracker to isolate the relevant drives within a scenario from concurrent activities happening simultaneously. Subsequently, a set of potential candidate scenarios is detected across a collection of driving sequences, with each individual sequence serving as a unique positive sample for the specific maneuver. These candidates are formed by segmenting sequences based on the identified start and finish points. To assess the distinctiveness of the different test sequences intended for the same label, an ensemble of pairwise comparisons is conducted using an agreement coefficient calculated on the annotations of each frame within those sequences finally, an automated six-stage procedure for label detection and scenario extraction across multiple driving contexts is proposed.

This paper introduces a channel estimation enhancement for Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) systems that employ a code division multiple access (CDMA) scheme. It addresses two key scenarios found in modern communication systems: (a) when the cyclic prefix is truncated to accommodate bandwidth efficiency, and (b) when hardware impairments cause signal distortion. In both cases, subsequent data symbols are integrated into the estimation process to improve the quality of recovery. The method assumes a multi-user environment with a sufficiently long antenna array relative to spatial degrees of freedom. The proposed ELM framework undergoes rigorous evaluation through simulations, comparing it against state-of-the-art algorithms. The results demonstrate that this ELM-based approach surpasses existing methods in channel estimation accuracy, particularly under conditions of shortened cyclic prefixes and imperfect hardware conditions.

When subject to quantum mechanics, standard interpretations suggest that projective measurements are the standard tool for state collapse. Nevertheless, recent research indicates that non-projective measurements can mimic projective measurements under specific conditions: this is possible whenever the measurement occurs within a sequence of completely positive and trace-preserving (CPTP) operations, or when the measurement strength is extremely weak. This paper demonstrates that such equivalences also hold during certain types of irreversible state transformations defined as non-unitary or dissipative processes. This finding offers a fresh perspective on how the measurement state can permeate reality independent of the specific mechanism or dynamics that introduced it.

We prove the rigidity of bounded, abelian $ \G7 $ -instantons defined on noncompact manifolds with compact boundary. As a consequence, we demonstrate that any small symplectic deformation, with no change, preserves the isometry group for closed, basic G2 instantons. This result serves as the G2 analogue of LeBrun's finding regarding self-dual and anti-self-dual instantons in the context of compact 4-dimensional manifolds.

Although contact tracing is an established public health strategy for curbing infectious disease transmission, widespread implementation risks eroding civil liberties and creating conditions for government mass surveillance initiatives. While existing research primarily examines how to enhance public adoption of tracing apps, a significant gap remains in understanding how to mitigate government surveillance risks without compromising tracing efficacy. To address this, we introduce a new decentralized, privacy-focused protocol that enables the public to verify whether their personal data is accessible to officials. The core mechanism involves storing all personal contact tracing data on a decentralized blockchain network, thereby eliminating reliance on any single government entity. Utilizable with standard smartphones, the proposed solution empowers citizens with full control and transparency regarding their personal information while maintaining the ability to support active contact tracing operations.

Decoherence is a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics that explains how independent subsystems interact and entangle. In a recent study, the authors revisited the Einstein-Podolsky Rosen paradox from the standpoint of decoherence, coining the term "decoherent collapse." This concept posits that a subsystem's internal decoherence induces correlated transformations in strongly correlated other subsystems. Specifically, if two quantum systems share a singlet state, decoherence in one results in an effective "measurement" of the other. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that "decoherent collapse" offers a clear explanation for the non-local behavior observed in quantum systems.

This study introduces a programming language, Natorc, designed to demonstrate how translating higher-level language constructs into a lower-level core can support verification of correctness. We argue that program properties established on the abstract, higher-level version can serve as a foundation to verify an equivalent property on the concrete implementation. The approach involves developing two versions of each concrete language stage and its corresponding abstract counterpart and establishing mappings between them to facilitate mutual translation and property expression. The validity theorems for our proof methodology are established, and specific illustrative examples demonstrate the methodology's utility. Additionally, the paper includes a higher-level abstract interpreter, which functions as both an optimizer and a tool for automatically driving the translations required to verify the concrete abstract interpreter's behavior.

Current 3D human pose estimation methods rely on a two-stage approach, utilizing a heat map generator followed by pose refinement, which often result in accuracy limitations. We propose an end-to-end single-stage method that boosts accuracy and speeds up the inference. The core innovation is a new loss function, named Heat-map Error-guided Learning, that leverages heat-map errors from the coding layer to automatically correct code-decoder weights. This dynamically reconfigures the coding space to reduce heat-map prediction errors and enhances model accuracy. We further apply model pruning to eliminate redundant parameters without compromising performance. We evaluated our method on the 3D Human Body Capture (H2BF) Challenge dataset. Compared to the standard two-stage baseline, our approach achieves a mean per-joint coordinate error (MPJPE) of 8.97 mm on the public validation set—an 11.7% improvement—and 8.58 mm on the private test set, a 10.5% improvement, respectively. We also reduced the model size by 42.5% with negligible impact on accuracy, attaining a speedup of 4.5x relative to the original two-stage method. Accurate travel time forecasting plays a vital role in traffic management and support for route planning applications. Current research predominantly employs deep learning solutions to estimate travel times directly from historical logs, relying on convolutions or recurrents to process sequential data, yet these methods typically demand substantial computational resources. Furthermore, when travel times serve as residual corrections to free-flow speeds, both data collection and application phases are less resource-intensive but exhibit lower accuracy. This study evaluates a gradient boosting decision tree approach that calculates travel times to act as adjustments for free-flow speed assessments, utilizing fewer data dependencies than direct estimation models while achieving a ninefold reduction in computational cost relative to them and demonstrating performance superior to graph-neural-network alternatives.

This paper proposes a framework to evaluate counterfactual fairness without relying on specific assumptions regarding the data-generating process. We demonstrate how causal inference techniques can generate counterfactual data points by examining the relationship between the predicted class labels and the action variable. This framework is applied to assess the fairness of a classification action in determining outcomes. Notably, our method applies to the black-box scenario where access to the specific classifier is unavailable to the analyst. We apply this approach to the Adult Census Income dataset, analyzing fairness outcomes across different gender subgroups within the data.

Future-generation radio telescopes, characterized by their massive data processing demands, require significant computational efforts to maintain data quality standards and handle volume effectively. This necessity has heightened the importance of local data processing at observatories, which in turn demands a robust and reliable infrastructure. This article details the computational environment and its associated infrastructure developed at the Jansky Very Large Array (VLA). It describes a flexible, cost-effective solution that leverages modern, local supercomputing models to address current challenges while remaining future-proof for upcoming instruments and software needs. The JANS machine, a recent, high-performance computing platform based on the new VLA BlueFraming Model, is introduced and compared alongside existing local resources. Additionally, the required modifications to current pipelines, made effective by integrating VLA's upgraded infrastructure, are reviewed.

This study examines the impact of secondary frequency control on small-signal dynamic stability within inverter-dominated networks. These equations are coupled with control loop dynamics representing both primary frequency control and grid-tied $P$-$V$ + $Q$-$U$ devices. To capture fast transient behaviors, a high-fidelity linear model incorporating fast capacitor dynamics is developed for analysis. Through this linearization, a crucial insight emerges regarding frequency control loops: their convergence to steady-state operating points is a prerequisite for stabilizing voltage profiles. Specifically, if secondary control does not stabilize the network, voltage oscillations persist indefinitely. Conversely, successful secondary control acts as a stabilizing mechanism that damps these oscillations and ensures robust system behavior. These findings are validated using simulations on an IEEE 38-node test feeder augmented with renewable energy sources.

This work addresses the challenge of achieving non-intrusive security in a newly emerging class of connected cyber-physical (CP) systems. Defined by their integrated cyber and physical components, these systems present distinct vulnerabilities across both the internal structure and external environment. The proposed framework recognizes two critical dimensions: (1) the system's internal components, divided into a control layer that executes actions and a sensing layer responsible for providing data to the controller; and (2) the system's external context, encompassing the surrounding environment and threats posed by malicious actors. Crucially, because the control layer relies entirely on sensor input, malicious input can force unsafe operational commands. Recognizing that non-intrusive approaches are essential to avoid degrading performance, we developed a secure estimation methodology utilizing an unsupervised learning technique. This approach detects ill-sensed states without prior knowledge of specific attacks. Validated through simulations on a double integrator model, the findings confirm that the developed unsupervised learning approach can indeed detect malicious sensing states without the need for prior attack information.

Solar acoustic waves traveling across the Sun's global meridional circulation paths can reveal horizontal flow dynamics. Compressing 4D light field (LF) images presents a challenging task due to the difficulty light field cameras have in handling noise. Additionally, this autoencoder utilizes a quantization network to handle image quantization. Experimental evaluations indicate that our method outperforms established techniques regarding both noise resilience and compression efficiency, as measured by both the noise-agnostic PSNR metric and the noise-aware NMSE metric.

Cross-lingual information retrieval (CIR) facilitates access to web content across different languages, but it is often hindered by the difficulty of achieving perfect user input. Our analysis demonstrates that Spherical TSNE, when utilizing the Student's t-distribution, produces more accurate local proximity estimates than both standard T-SNE and a broad category of linear dimensionality reduction methods. Furthermore, these findings suggest that Spherical TSNE is capable of capturing local proximity with greater fidelity than conventional linear techniques as well.

The $B_{c}$-meson features a novel double-charm structure; consequently, its associated hadrons exhibit longer proper decay lengths than charm-related particles. By analyzing simulated events involving $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$\,TeV, we measured the decay mass threshold for $B_{c}$-hadrons and found a mean proper decay distance of approximately 480 $\mu$m. This observed value surpasses the lengths measured for charm and bottom hadrons, providing experimental validation for the predicted $B_{c}$-meson structure. Furthermore, we assessed the sensitivity achieved by LHC experiments, demonstrating that future experiments at high-energy proton-proton collisions can determine these properties with even greater precision.

We introduce a novel method for analyzing color-based interactions within the classes of a topological space, enabling the computation of persistent homology through an extended matrix-based approach that accounts for these colors. This technique serves as a foundational step toward creating a "persistent homology with colors" concept and includes a section on applying colored persistence calculations to the geometric modeling of the human brain.

This study addresses the biternary power allocation problem within the context of large interference networks, where the number of active transmitters is comparable to or greater than the number of receivers. We introduce binary power control as the mechanism for activating a single transmit antenna per receiver; specifically, each node chooses between power levels of $P$ and $0$. Our approach relies on the "nearest neighbor" principle, where the node closest to a given receiver is empowered, while all others remain silent. We demonstrate that for networks with random, independent transmitter and receiver locations, the aggregate interference power under this scheme converges to the maximum possible random location configuration for binary power allocation, which in turn approaches the same limit as $N \to \infty$. Numerical simulations suggest that even when locations are not randomly distributed or independent, this specific implementation achieves near-optimal performance relative to optimal power allocation, albeit at just a fraction of the computational cost.

Financial audits are a critical component of the accounting framework, and a primary objective of the audit team is to identify and correct errors within a client's financial records. A key challenge for these teams is balancing individual standards of rigor against client constraints regarding costs and accounting software limitations. To address these competing priorities, this study proposes a decision-making framework utilizing a multi-criteria evaluation of audit procedures. This approach integrates the new grouping method for numerical data into the framework specifically for procedure selection. By applying the group PROMETHEE II method along with individual mass functions for each criterion, the model accommodates diverse auditor interests and their corresponding uncertainty levels. Using the framework's output to finalize audit decisions, this method enables an auditee to express confidence in specific line items while identifying others as belonging to a specific category of interest.

This paper outlines a flexible, precise, and straightforward approach for simulating arbitrary point processes. The proposed "Acceptance Rejection Stitching" technique leverages the fact that a unique simulation method can be established for any point process that simulates a Poisson process. When the target Poisson process is intractable, an approximate version is used instead; the approximation is accepted with calculated probability to produce an sample-correct Poisson process. The method accepts individual event samples, generating a derived correct Poisson process. Finally, the output combines segments of simulations from various methods using strategic stitching, and from these, extracts relevant event samples to form the final simulation for the general point process. The paper also presents multiple equivalent formulations of this algorithm. Extensive numerical evaluations confirm that the method remains highly effective and efficient even under extreme conditions. The study concludes by demonstrating how the approach applies the same methodology to other point process models.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) introduces low-level corrections to quantum mechanics, emerging from specific frameworks within string theory and quantum gravity. Recent investigations have derived stochastic equations of motion from the GUP-induced quantum framework. The present study demonstrates that these equations yield a specific set of Galilean transformations; notably, the resulting shift in the energy-momentum variables under GUP aligns with what the Lorentz transformations imply. This finding suggests a remarkable mathematical and physical correspondence between the two distinct transformation schemes across the quantum and relativistic regimes.

This study examines the scheduling of multiple sequential tasks within a heterogeneous, multitasking computing environment. Unlike previous research, we allow processors to dynamically share capacity with adjacent processors, with each task manager capable of determining the split. While total system processing power remains constant, this capability enables sub-tasks to be executed in parallel across processors. We demonstrate that even minor fluctuations in sharing strategies can drastically change scheduling outcomes. To address this, we develop an efficient simulation approach for optimal single-level, credit-based credit scheduling. We then analyze the relationship between processing capacity sharing and task completion times. Finally, we evaluate how sharing ratios influence both the probability and expected duration of task delays (backlog).

Simulated experiments involving locomotion over soft surfaces in various terrains demonstrate that a feedback-controlled hopping strategy improves the robot's ability to track planned trajectories compared to open-loop control. These feedback mechanisms also facilitate the recovery from disturbances and enable the parametric analysis of the dynamic model to adapt controllers for soft-ground interactions. Specifically, under certain conditions, soft-ground dynamics can be effectively modeled as a linear time-invariant (LTI) system; when this model is integrated with the controller, the ability to track a broader range of trajectories is achieved.

Firmware updates are critical for the operational maintenance of any IoT deployment. However, broadcast failures frequently hinder these processes in expansive environments, and concurrent transmissions (CT) can cause significant signal interference, rendering this solution unviable. This work reexamines the role of CT, demonstrating that it can actually enhance both scalability and firmware delivery reliability for large-scale IoT deployments. We present **UCT**, a novel, lightweight, and fully distributed protocol for uplinking IoT devices using CT. By leveraging a randomized backoff mechanism, UCT allows transmissions to overlap constructively, avoiding destructive collisions. We conducted extensive real-world experiments across IoT fields ranging from indoor to outdoor environments, testing scenarios with 50, 100, and 300 devices. The results indicate that UCT achieves 90% higher scalability and attains 20% to 40% improved reliability compared to traditional non-overlapping transmissions.

In process mining, we frequently analyze how actual execution processes deviate from their design. Although the field has extensively explored the generation and manipulation of linear alignments for this comparison, process structures often resemble decision trees more than they do simple sequences. To address this, we introduce tree-ordered alignments, which generalize the alignment concept to tree-structured objects and encompass infix and postfix approaches as special cases. By performing orders independently on individual trees rather than creating a single linear trace of the entire execution, these methods offer distinct process behavior insights while preserving valid alignment properties. To support these concepts, the authors define the necessary preliminaries and two types of tree alignments, the `TAA` algorithm, and a `TAA` algorithm that generalizes infix and postfix to resolve the computational problem. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate how tree alignments can compute a tree of operations between two execution trees to identify shared and unique steps, and show that `TAA` effectively computes these tree alignments efficiently. Finally, the authors apply tree alignments to two key problems involving shared and unique steps between execution trees, and demonstrate their potential for practical use in process mining applications.

We suggest a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) approach for radio propagation modeling that learns to predict signal attenuation from transmitter power, the receiver's location, and a 3D cube surrounding the site rendered into a volume map. Our results indicate such learned models can significantly outperform traditional empirical propagation models. Furthermore, employing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to convert site 3D maps into site 2D images as model inputs yields performance gains over using only the 3D volume input. Finally, a comparative performance evaluation demonstrates that this proposed method is effective across various propagation environments.

While contemporary temporal planning systems have achieved significant success, they often overlook the validation of both their outputs and the planning problem itself. We introduce such a validation tool, which can confirm the correctness of a problem's data and the accuracy of a planner's algorithm and plan generation, demonstrating its utility with several illustrative cases.

This paper investigates the economic and operational impacts of temporal resolution in investment models for future systems integrating renewable sources and flexible gas capacities. Utilizing the European power landscape, we demonstrate that generation capacity misallocation costs rise significantly with time step resolution, escalating from 60% at 60-minute intervals to over 98.8% when refined to 15-minute steps. These misallocation errors also lead to substantial increases in long-term investment expenses. Our analysis attributes these phenomena to model biases that underestimate the durations of zero-output periods and non-zero production periods. To address this, we propose an adjustment method that effectively reduces these costs.

Refactoring tools currently struggle with ambiguous task descriptions, specifically regarding the selection of an appropriate search term. To address this, we propose a novel approach that leverages Natural Language Processing (NLP) to suggest optimal search terms for software modification tasks. Our underlying hypothesis is that valuable search terms are prevalent within the current implementation of a task, particularly those situated near critical code locations identified by TaskWeb. To operationalize this, we developed two algorithms: TextRank and POSRank, which analyze tasks using specific NLP metrics. To facilitate comparison, we assembled a dataset comprising approximately 1,000 search term instances across 300 tasks derived from two prominent open-refactoring projects, with these search terms manually tagged as either unsuitable or suitable. Our empirical findings demonstrate that the proposed methods successfully extract numerous viable search terms. Furthermore, we evaluated and compared the efficacy of our proposed algorithms against a baseline method derived from prior research.

This paper presents an experimental investigation into ultrasound-assisted fluidization of viscoelastic gels, focusing on the temporal evolution of granular convection velocities and suspension homogeneity. These dynamics are linked to varying temporal profiles of acoustic intensity, which are derived from non-steady wave interference patterns. The results reveal a distinct shift in fluidization behavior: while low ultrasound intensity fails to sustain fluid motion once the driving source is deactivated, sufficient intensity successfully overcomes viscoelastic yield stresses to establish fully developed granular convection. Furthermore, this study analyzes how rheo-acoustic gel properties influence the onset of oscillatory post-failure motion in fluidized media.

In domains like law and finance, where document classification involves critical outcomes, it is essential to comprehend the rationale behind machine learning predictions. Consequently, this study introduces an approach to generate local explanations for natural language processing tasks, specifically tailored to explain classification decisions over documents to users. employing the Anshali method to create these explanations, it is shown user comprehension of classification rationale can be dramatically bolstered. These explanations serve effectively as a basis for identifying misleading examples and can also support the training of more equitable classifiers. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that Anshali can scale to manage extensive vocabulary sizes typically associated with document datasets while maintaining its effectiveness.

This study examines a large market where agents utilize public ratings to facilitate utility measurement and matchings achieve stability. The core question addressed is how these rating mechanisms affect the resulting matching and associated agent utilities within such systems. To investigate this, we introduce a model where an agent's utility for a potential partner is determined by the sum of their base utility and the squared discrepancy between their rating and that partner's rating offered by them. Under this framework, we derive and examine a specific stable matching algorithm. Our analysis demonstrates that when the number of agents is sufficiently large, these public ratings converge in probability to the true average utilities for each pair. Furthermore, this rating-based outcome is shown to approximate the utility distribution of a standard stable matching derived from the agents' true utilities, with a maximum per-agent variation that diminishes as total population size expands.

This paper presents SummScore, an automated evaluation metric for English text summarization. The objective is to create a rapid, reliable, and cost-effective method to assess summary quality that strongly aligns with human ratings, offering a superior alternative to existing metrics. SummScore enhances the summary diversity of current evaluation metrics, thereby achieving a significantly higher correlation with human scores. The metric operates by generating multiple summaries of varying lengths and evaluating the structural and semantic coherence of each sequence. The findings indicate that SummScore correlates exceptionally well with human assessments across summaries produced by diverse models. We make our SummScore implementation publicly available to facilitate its integration into future summarization research endeavors.

Recovering signals from limited and noisy measurements is a critical challenge in many scientific domains, particularly where cross-correlated data reduces the number of independently measurable sparse signals. The cross-correlation level between available data directly impacts the maximum sparsity that can be recovered. This study introduces a sparsity recovery framework that utilizes a pre-trained model to generate inferences for a new model instance. Our method is designed to leverage all available correlated data when handling multiple measurement sets, thereby improving the utilization of cross-correlated information. Pre-training a model across varied data sets enables the efficient handling of large volumes of real-world information without the need for additional computational resources. The approach is evaluated on real data from the IceCube neutrino observatory, which tracks neutrinos by reconstructing the trajectories of muons. The results indicate that fully exploiting all correlated data can enable the recovery of sparsity levels up to 20% higher than previously possible.

BeVFusion (Decentralized Volume Fusion) is a method that converts different sensor data into oriented LiDAR-like voxels and operates in a decentralized manner to achieve object detection. The framework's main advantage is its detection performance improvement, particularly when one or both sensors fail. Furthermore, the approach facilitates easy data fusion of various sensors and voxels. Experimental results demonstrate that the method outperforms state-of-the-art detection techniques.

This study examines how deterministically modeled turbulence dissipates within a viscous fluid at small scales, utilizing the stochastic, energy-conserving fluctuating hydrodynamics (FH) equation. We demonstrate that, similar to classical Kolmogorov phenomenology, energy in finite-size domains dominated by turbulence is primarily lost through scales comparable to the computational box dimensions. However, the FH equation reveals that fluctuations and deterministic velocity fields decouple near the resolution cutoff ($\ell = L_{box}$), meaning deterministic viscosity and the resulting deterministic Navier-Stokes equation suffice to describe transport at these small scales. Consequently, determining the exact statistical properties of turbulence at scales smaller than the box width $L_{box}$ reduces to solving a driven diffusive system. This finding clarifies the link between deterministic turbulence models and the statistical mechanics of fluid flow.

We present the findings from experiments designed to study laser light scattering and heating within a fluid container subjected to natural convection. The sample cell is maintained under a constant temperature difference, establishing a well-defined large-scale circulation pattern within the fluid. When illuminated, the fluid exhibits reproducible, large-scale structures in its heat distribution, which manifest as distinct features in the laser's diffraction patterns. Additionally, we analyzed the fluctuations of light intensity traversing a vertical path through a non-heating fluid situated next to the convection cell. Both horizontal and vertical trajectories through this adjacent area reveal patterns that mirror the temperature fluctuations and flow dynamics occurring inside the thermal cell.

Although numerous studies have recently concentrated on design recommendation systems leveraging external knowledge bases, there are still several critical gaps. These deficiencies include a lack of conclusion reliability, sparseness in relevant context, insufficient recommendation precision, and low recall for pertinent proposals. This paper introduces a multi-pass and multi-view (PM2V) methodology designed to enhance recall and proposal stability across domains by cross-referencing multiple relevant contexts for each query. Specifically, the PM2V framework utilizes two main mechanisms: (PM2C) a multi-conclusion approach to generate robust outcomes through aggregated relevant contexts, reducing reliance on any single path; (PM2R) a multi-recommendation system that simultaneously suggests diverse yet suitable designs to avoid dependency on a solitary optimal choice. Both methods feature iterative refinement loops that iteratively re-evaluate and fine-tune recommendations. Additionally, the study introduces a novel E-V* embedding model that effectively maps queries and external knowledge bases into a shared semantic space. Experimental validation across three real-world scenarios demonstrates that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

H-STREAM represents a novel architecture designed for a large-scale, reconfigurable IoT Internet, integrating smart meters within residential environments to monitor, regulate, and react to energy consumption in real time. Given the high transmission velocity and volume of streaming data from these millions of sensors, managing this influx efficiently is critical. This paper introduces HH-STREAM, an end-to-end framework optimized for intelligent reconfiguration across vast distributed sensor deployments. By leveraging recent breakthroughs in parallel and recurrent deep learning—specifically Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks—alongside established strategies for batch and real-time model retraining, the system achieves superior prediction and trend analysis. This research validates that applying these flexible retraining techniques significantly enhances monitoring capabilities, with real-world deployments on reconfigurable smart homes demonstrating a substantial reduction in energy bills.

Performance is evaluated using standard norms in both continuous and discrete time domains. The functorial clustering scheme developed in prior work is expanded to accommodate single-linkage clustering, though existing formulations prove ineffective when applied to large-scale datasets. To resolve scalability bottlenecks and address data sparsity, this research introduces expansion strategies for the functorial scheme specifically for linkage clustering. These expansions derive new formulas capable of estimating cluster cardinality and volume by leveraging Mummery simplices' persistent homology attributes, while also incorporating sampling protocols to guarantee that every simplex is selected with equal probability.

Deep learning-based tensor completion (TC) methods have gained popularity in video prediction and restoring, but relying on global tensor structures renders them unable to handle motion in video streams, which severely limits their performance. To address this, we introduce a new strategy grounded in an enhanced understanding of both data and motion, launching a class of learning-driven TC algorithms. First, we utilize recent advancements in motion perception to detect movement across frames and partition the tensor into multiple sub-tensors accordingly. Next, leveraging the inherent low-rank nature of each sub-tensor, we develop a dynamic sub-tensor recombination technique that outperforms the static recombination found in existing solutions. Finally, to further enhance performance, we present one-step sub-tensor projections to increase the number of observations utilized within each iteration. Extensive experiments on various public datasets show that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art TC approaches in video interpolation, which greatly enhances the quality of generated video sequences.

We establish that whenever a braiding matrix $M$ corresponds to a real reflection group with rank $G \geq 4$, the associated Nichols algebra $\mathcal{B}(V_M)$ is infinite dimensional. This result supports the conjecture previously put forward by Andruskiw-Wade and Wang regarding these structures.

This study presents numerical simulations modeling hydrodynamic turbulence driven by inertial waves, utilizing periodic forcing to excite these waves. By forcing the system into a steady state, the dynamics align with the predictions of inertial wave turbulence. Within this regime, hydrodynamic energy follows the anisotropic $k^{-4}$ equipartition law originally derived by Goncharov and Elskens. Furthermore, the results demonstrate clear non-linear energy transfer between wavenumbers within the inertial wave dispersion relation. These findings confirm experimental and previous numerical evidence of both energy and enstencil energy power spectra.

This study examines the graph normalization technique developed by Balcan et al.\ (2015), originally designed for generating approximate solutions to the Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) problem and addressing k-Set Partitioning and Set Covering. Our contributions are twofold: first, we establish that the normalization process inherently serves as a valid dual decomposition of a linear program equivalent to the MWIS problem; second, we demonstrate that dual infeasibility for the Set Covering and $k$-Set Partitioning problems inherent to specific instances can yield their unbounded dual objective. Consequently, these findings clarify the limitations of the Balcan et al.\ approach and impose strict boundaries on its applicability to $k$-Set Partitioning and Set Covering. Furthermore, we prove dual unboundedness for specific graphs relevant to the Set Covering and $k$-Set Partitioning problems, demonstrating the fundamental inability of this normalization method to produce bounded, feasible dual solutions for such instances.

This study analyzes the Dirac Hamiltonian within a two-dimensional periodic electric potential subjected to an orthogonal magnetic field, focusing on both bulk properties and those influenced by graphene lattice specifics. We demonstrate that when Landau Levels undergo double periodic modulation, they generate various types of oscillations: primary periodicity matching the crystal lattice, secondary oscillations with a period derived from the sum of the lattice periods, and Fuchs' oscillations with a period inversely proportional to the magnetic field strength. This paper examines the amplitude dependence of the Landau Level energy peaks regarding lattice potential periods, focusing on the unique scenario of strongly coupled coupling between double periodic oscillations, where the lattice period reciprocals align. This coupling, influenced by the graphene lattice, leads to distinct charge carrier modulation patterns across different Landau Level energy peaks. This modulation varies by carrier type (electrons or holes), Land Level index, and charge valley, offering a potential mechanism for selective carrier modulation and enabling the controlled manipulation of specific charge carriers within single-layer structures.

Articulated Neural Rendering (AR) introduces a new neural framework designed to render diverse moving objects through neural networks. While previous methods like Functional Motion Rendering (FMR) rely on fixed, predefined keyframes for optimization and require interpolation for intermediate states—an approach that results in a disconnect between blended prior functions and leads to poor image fidelity—AR takes a fundamentally different approach by optimizing every frame jointly. Articulated Neural Rendering represents each object as a pair of neural functions (one governing appearance, the other motion) and optimizes these across all target frames simultaneously using a generative model of their relationship, thereby achieving consistent high-quality results on static, partially observable, and fully observable objects down to pixel-accurate detail. To facilitate high-resolution rendering and enhance feature reuse across frames, AR implements neural feature caching, a technique that stores computed features and retrieves them upon similar view conditions during optimization to boost efficiency.

This paper addresses few-shot semantic parsing, aiming to generate natural language utterances with accurate logical forms across numerous unseen tasks given only a limited number of training examples per task. Although current methods are competitive, their effectiveness lags significantly behind standard semantic parsing due to slow convergence in such data-scarce environments. We propose a novel framework to expedite this learning process through two primary strategies: (1) leveraging vast amounts of unsupervised data to fully understand language structure and semantics, and (2) fully exploiting few-shot samples across diverse tasks to accelerate the rapid construction of an effective parsing model for new tasks. Specifically, we first train a multi-lingual BERT to create rich semantic embeddings for few-shot task data and unsupervised corpus data. Next, we feed these embeddings into a prediction network, which outputs an initial set of logical forms for the few-shot data; we then refine the model using an end-to-end execution-driven pipeline. Finally, we fine-tune a sequence-to-sequence network, initially trained on a broad logical form dataset, by replacing its standard input embeddings with those from the few-shot samples. This upgraded model is then refined via execution feedback to build a robust task-specific form generator. Extensive tests confirm the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a 4-point improvement over existing methods on standard English datasets. Furthermore, our method successfully performs zero-shot multilingual semantic parsing and provides the first non-execution-based framework for few-shot English semantic parsing.

The topological silicene has garnered significant interest for potential spintronic applications, though its spintronic traits are highly sensitive to structural distortions caused by impurities. This study explores how topological silicene decorated with manganese (Mn) atoms at various sites—including the center bridge (SB) and off-bridge (OB) positions—affects its spintronic characteristics using spin-polarized transport simulations within the Landauer-B\"uttiker framework. We examine both the spin-dependent conductance in systems with single impurities and the tunneling current in double-impurity configurations. Our results indicate that the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter ($U$) is location-dependent, being substantially higher when Mn is placed at the SB or OB positions compared to lower values at the SB. This indicates a direct correlation between $U$ and Mn atomic positions. Regarding conductance, systems featuring OB-position Mn atoms exhibit a dominant spin-polarized peak, whereas SB-position Mn configurations display multiple spin-degenerate peaks. In the study of dipolar conductance, OB-manganese arrangements generate multiple spin-dependent conductance peaks, while those with SB-manganese atoms result in fewer such peaks. Furthermore, when comparing two distinct transport pathways, OB-manganese configurations allow for two conductance peaks, while SB-manganese configurations result in four conductance peaks. These findings suggest that topological silicene, modified by Mn atoms, offers promising applications for spintronic devices.

Sgr A East is the Galactic centre direction's most prominent radio supernova remnant, yet its explosion distance remains uncertain. We applied the non-parametric Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to determine the source's distance using multi-frequency (0.33–2.1 GHz) spectral index data. Specifically, we employed independent priors regarding the free electron gas expansion model and the structure of the magnetic field within the object to generate distance probability density functions. Our findings indicate that Sgr A East is located at approximately 5 kiloparsecs from the Galactic nucleus (with uncertainty of ±1.1 kpc). This distance measurement aligns closely with independent results derived via the method of spectral synthesis.
